Catalytic N–H Bond Formation Promoted by a Ruthenium Hydride Complex Bearing a Redox-Active Pyrimidine-Imine Ligand.

# Sangmin Kim, Junho Kim, Hongyu Zhong, Grace B. Panetti and Paul J. Chirik*

Department of Chemistry, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544, United States

ABSTRACT: The synthesis of a piano-stool ruthenium hydride, [(η5-C5Me5)Ru(PmIm)H] (PmIm = (N-(1,3,5-trimethylphenyl)-1-(pyrimidin-2-yl)ethan-1-imine) for the dual purpose of catalytic dihydrogen activation and subsequent hydrogen atom transfer for the formation of weak chemical bonds is described. Introduction of a neutral, potentially redox-active PmIm supporting ligand was designed to eliminate the possibility of deleterious C(sp2)–H reductive coupling and elimination that has been identified as a deactivation pathway with related rhodium and iridium catalysts. Treatment of  [(η5-C5Me5)RuCl2]n with one equivalent PmIm ligand in the presence of zinc and sodium methoxide resulted in isolation of the diruthenium complex, [(η5-C5Me5)Ru(PmIm)]2, arising from C–C bond formation between two PmIm chelates. Addition of H2 to the ruthenium dimer under both thermal and blue light irradiation conditions furnished the targeted hydride, [(η5- C5Me5)Ru(PmIm)H] which has a relatively weak DFT-calculated Ru–H bond dissociation free energy (BDFE) of 47.9 kcal/mol. Addition of TEMPO to [(η5-C5Me5)Ru(PmIm)H] generated the 17-electron metalloradical, [(η5-C5Me5)Ru(PmIm)], which was characterized by EPR spectroscopy. The C–C bond forming process was reversible as irradiation of [(η5-C5Me5)Ru(PmIm)]2 generated [(η5-C5Me5)Ru(PmIm)H] and a piano-stool ruthenium complex containing an enamide ligand derived from H-atom abstraction from the PmIm chelate. Equilibration studies were used to establish an experimental estimate of the effective Ru–H BDFE and a value of 50.8 kcal/mol was obtained, in agreement with the observed loss of H2 and the DFT-computed value. The ruthenium hydride was an effective catalyst for the thermal catalytic hydrogenation of TEMPO, acridine and a cobalt-imido complex and for the selective reduction of azobenzene to diphenylhydrazine using H2 as the terminal reductant, highlighting the role of this complex is catalytic weak bond formation using H2 as the stoichiometric reductant.

INTRODUCTION Transition metal complexes that enable both the activation of H2 and subsequent hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) have been applied to the synthesis of weak chemical bonds.1-5 Among several types of these complexes, (η5-C5Me5)-supported, piano-stool group 9 metal hydrides with L,X-type chelate ligands, [(η5-C5Me5)M(L,X)H] (M = Rh, Ir; (L,X) = 2-phenylpyridine, benzo[h]quinone) first developed by Norton and coworkers,6 have shown remarkable activity in the catalytic reduction of various compounds using H2 as the terminal reductant (Figure 1a).7-14 Because most HAT processes rely on reagents as hydrogen atom sources that generate stoichiometric quantities of waste,15,16 use of H2 as the terminal reductant is preferred for improved atom economy and overall sustainability. One feature of [(η5-C5Me5)M(L,X)H) compounds is the relatively low M–H bond dissociation free energies in the range of 52-61 kcal/mol,7,10,13 which are strong enough to promote the cleavage of H2 but weak enough to promote subsequent HAT to the desired substrate (Figure 1a).7-14 These metal hydrides are also sufficiently basic (pKa > 30 in MeCN)7,10 so that deleterious protonation chemistry is suppressed.

Despite their catalytic performance in weak element-hydrogen bond formation, [(η5-C5Me5)M(L,X)H] compounds are hampered by competing catalyst deactivation pathways arising from thermal17 and photochemical10,13,17 C(sp2)–H reductive coupling and elimination reactions (Figure 1b). Ligand modifications have been applied by our group to improve the stability of this class of catalysts, but nevertheless these processes persist.10,18 As a result, a new catalyst design strategy was developed whereby the L,X-type supporting ligand in the piano-stool metal hydride was replaced with neutral ligands to remove the driving force and possibility for reductive coupling and elimination. To maintain isoelectronic and isolobal precatalysts, this design principle necessitates a migration from group 9 metals to the group 8 triad (Figure 1b). Many examples of (η5-C5H5)- or (η5-C5Me5)-supported, pianostool group 8 metal hydrides have been reported and been applied to catalytic ionic hydrogenation reactions.19-25 However, the HAT reactivity of these compounds has not been thoroughly studied with the exception of the stoichiometric HAT reactivity of [(η5- C5H5)Ru(CO)2H] with trityl radical.26-29 Catalytic HAT activity using H2 as the terminal reductant by a group 8 metal hydride is elusive. By comparison to group 9 piano- stool hydrides that have M–H BDFEs in the range of 52-61 kcal/mol,7,10,13 [(η5-C5H5)Ru(CO)2H] has a relatively high Ru–H BDFE that is >65 kcal/mol26-28 rendering HAT reactions from this complex to form weak bonds thermodynamically prohibitive.

Two approaches were considered to lower the Ru–H BDFE (Figure 2a). Because a M–H BDFE is determined by the difference between the ground state energies of M–H and M• + H•, increasing the ground state energy of the M–H (destabilization of M–H) or decreasing the ground state energy of the M• + H• (stabilization of M•) lowers the overall M–H BDFE. While the former is undesirable because the instability of the parent metal hydride can induce side reactions, the latter is preferrable. Thus, stabilization of the post- HAT metalloradical was targeted as the primary ligand and ultimately catalyst design principle.

*Figure 2. (a) Two strategies to lower a M–H BDFE. (b) A ruthenium hydride with a redox-active pyrimidine-imine (PmIm) ligand and its properties.*

One method to stabilize metalloradicals is to introduce redox-active ligands – those that undergo reversible electron transfer with the transition metal.30-34 It was envisioned that delocalization of an unpaired electron in a post-HAT, 17-electron product would induce stabilization of the compound which in turn would lower the M–H BDFE.35 An alternative statement of this concept is modulation of the redox potential as described by the Bordwell equation. Among various types of redox-active ligands, pyrimidine-imine (PmIm) ligands were selected (Figure 2b). These nitrogen-based chelates are neutral but structurally similar to the N,C-type chelates used with the group 9 metal catalysts6-14 with established redox-activity.30,31 In addition, the two nitrogens in the pyridimine ring would maintain nitrogen-coordination and prevent rollover cyclometallation in the event of ring dissociation.36 Here we describe the synthesis, characterization and HAT reactivity of the piano-stool ruthenium hydride,  [(η5-C5Me5)Ru(PmIm)H] (Figure 2b). Despite a relatively low DFT-calculated Ru–H BDFE of 47.9 kcal/mol in acetonitrile and an experimental value of ~50 kcal/mol, both thermal (60 °C) and photochemical (465 nm light) stability were observed. A 17-electron mononuclear ruthenium compound following HAT was detected by EPR spectroscopy, and the redox-activity of the pyrimidine-imine was supported by DFT calculations and observed dimerization reactivity. The new C–C bond that arises from coupling of the two pyrimidine-imine ligands was homolytically cleaved under photochemical conditions to regenerate the monomeric 17-electron compound. These unique properties of the ruthenium hydride enabled catalytic, selective hydrogenation of TEMPO, azobenzene, acridine and a cobalt-imido complex under mild conditions by hydrogen atom transfer. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION Synthesis of a Piano-Stool Ruthenium Hydride and Reversible C–C Bond Formation of the Redox-Active Ligand. The synthesis of the targeted ruthenium hydride bearing a redox-active, neutral N,N-type chelate was attempted by addition of one equivalent of NaOMe to a mixture of in situ generated [(η5-C5Me5)RuCl]n and N- (1,3,5-trimethylphenyl)-1-(pyrimidin-2-yl)ethan-1-imine (PmIm, Scheme 1a). Following heating at 60 °C for 24 hours and recrystallization, a dark red crystalline solid was isolated in 35% yield and identified as the bimetallic ruthenium complex, [(η5- C5Me5)Ru(PmIm)]2 (1) as determined by NMR spectroscopy and single crystal X-ray diffraction (Scheme 1b). Analysis of the unpurified reaction mixture by 1H NMR spectroscopy revealed a singlet centered at −12.68 ppm, consistent with formation of the targeted ruthenium hydride. However, attempts to isolate the ruthenium hydride from the reaction mixture were unsuccessful due to it similar solubility to the remaining free ligand. The isolated bimetallic ruthenium complex can be viewed as arising from dimerization of the putative 17-electron compound, [(η5-C5Me5)Ru(PmIm)] (3) that would form following loss of hydrogen atom from the targeted hydride [(η5-C5Me5)Ru(PmIm)H] (2). The solid-state structure of 1 established a bimetallic ruthenium complex where each monomeric subunit is related by a center of inversion (Scheme 1b). Unlike most previously reported dimeric metal complexes obtained following HAT that contain metal-metal bonds,1,2,20,28,29,37-42 1 is bridged by a newly formed C–C bond between the ipso carbons of the PmIm ligands. Exposure of 1 to 4 atm of H2 generated the ruthenium hydride, [(η5- C5Me5)Ru(PmIm)H] (2) (Scheme 2a). When the hydrogenation reaction was conducted for 72 hours at 60 °C, 2 was obtained in 90% yield as determined by NMR spectroscopy with observation of a diagnostic ruthenium-hydride signal at -12.68 ppm in benzene-d6. Notably, this resonance is identical to the one observed in situ during the synthesis of 1. No side products or decomposition was observed at 60 °C highlighting the thermal stability of 2. The formation of 2 from 1 suggested that 1 dissociates into the 17-electron intermediate 3, which activates H2 to form 2. DFT computations established a relatively low Ru–H BDFE of 47.9 kcal/mol in acetonitrile at the B3LYP level of theory. This value compares favorably to the experimentally established M–H BDFEs of [(η5-C5H5)Ru(CO)2H] (65– 72 kcal/mol)26-28 and [(η5-C5Me5)Rh(ppy)H] (52.3 kcal/mol)7 in acetonitrile. Unfortunately, single crystals of 2 suitable for X-ray diffraction were not obtained as 1 was consistently isolated likely a result of loss of H2 over the course of the crystallization process.46,47 Inspired by this result, the conversion of 2 to 1 was investigated by heating a benzene solution of 2 at 60 °C for 7 days under an N2 atmosphere (Scheme 2a). Formation of 1 was observed by 1H NMR spectroscopy in 40% yield. Scheme 2. (a) Interconversion of 1 and [(η5-C5Me5)Ru(PmIm)H] (2) under thermal conditions and formation of a mononuclear 17- electron species [(η5-C5Me5)Ru(PmIm)] (3) by reaction of 2 and TEMPO. (b) Schematic description of the effective BDFE of 2 and

thermoneutrality of H2 activation and H2 release mediated by the ruthenium complex.

In the presence of 4 atm of H2, the thermal conversion of 1 to 2 reached 90% and established equilibrium (Scheme 2a). From these conditions, an equilibrium constant (Keq = [2]2/[1]PH2)48 was calculated as 0.122 atm-1, corresponding to a ΔGH2 ~ 1.2 kcal/mol and translating onto an approximate Ru–H BDFE of 50.8 kcal/mol (see S10 for more details). Also, the interconversion of 1 and 2 under thermal conditions further supports a relatively low Ru–H BDFE in the range of 52.0 kcal/mol of ΔGf°(H•) and a kinetic barrier for H2 evolution that imparts stability to 2, allowing its isolation (Scheme 2b).46 It is important to note that the experimentally established Ru– H BDFE in the interconversion of 1 and 2 is an effective BDFE that is distinct from a theoretical Ru–H BDFE, which is estimated as 47.9 kcal/mol by the DFT computation (Scheme 2b). Nevertheless, the low effective Ru-H BDFE below or close to 52 kcal/mol demonstrates the near thermoneutrality of H2 activation.48

(b) X-Band EPR spectrum of the unpurified reaction mixture of 2 and TEMPO recorded at 4 K in toluene. Attempts to generate the monomeric 17-electron ruthenium compound 3 were also explored. Addition of 1.5 equivalents of TEMPO to a benzene-d6 solution of 27,10 resulted in rapid formation of TEMPO–H (BDFEO–H = 65.2 kcal/mol)49 along with a paramagnetic ruthenium compound (Scheme 2a). The EPR spectrum (Figure 3a) recorded at 23 °C in benzene exhibited an isotropic signal (giso = 2.034), consistent with formation of the mononuclear ruthenium compound 3, similar to the spectroscopic data reported for related rhodium compounds.7,10 Also, the EPR spectrum (Figure 3b) recorded at 4 K in toluene exhibited an axial signal (gx = gy = 2.026, gz = 2.017), consistent with observations with a related ruthenium complex with delocalization of a free radical on the metal and the ligand.50 This view of the electronic structure is further supported by the DFT-computed Mulliken spin density plot (Figure 4).51 This electronic structure is likely the origin of the observed coupling of the ligands to form the C–C bond observed in 1. Although the dimerization of 3 to 1 occurred at room temperature, the slow conversion enabled detection of 3 by EPR spectroscopy. Addition of 4 atm H2 to a benzene-d6 solution of 3 at 60 °C resulted in complete*

conversion to 2, indicating the competency of 2 as a HAT catalyst using H2 as the terminal reductant (Scheme 2a).

*Figure 4. Mulliken spin density plot of 3.*

Although 2 was successfully formed under thermal conditions, the slow rate of conversion prompted exploration of alternative synthetic routes (Scheme 3). The electronic absorption spectrum of 1 recorded in benzene solution exhibited a band centered (λmax) at 434 nm (ε = 16,900 M-1cm-1), suggesting the potential for reactivity initiated by blue light (Scheme 3b). Irradiation of a benzene solution of 1 with a blue Kessil lamp for only 24 hours at 23 °C in the presence of 4 atm of H2 produced 2 in complete conversion (Scheme 3a). Continued irradiation of 2 with blue light for an additional 24 hours at 23 °C produced no change, demonstrating the improved photochemical stability of the piano-stool ruthenium hydride as compared to the rhodium and iridium analogs with L,X-type supporting ligands where C(sp2)–H reductive coupling and elimination were observed.10,13,1 TD-DFT calculations identified two vertical transitions with large oscillator strengths at 442 nm and 420 nm. Analysis of these transition indicated that the peaks of interest exhibited primarly metal-to-ligand charge transfer (MLCT) character with smaller contributions for d-d and intraligand charge transfer (ILCT) (Scheme 3b, Figures S26-S28).  In and attempt to determine the quantum yield of the conversion of dimer to monomer, the sources of monochromatic light were insufficiently strong at 435 nm to determine the amount of product generated. This corresponds to a quantum yield of <1% and is consistent with the observation of a reaction that requires irradiation with a Kessil lamp for 24 hours to reach completion.

The synthesis of 2 from photodriven hydrogenation of 1 motivated additional studies exploring photochemical methods to access 3 (Scheme 4a). Irradiation of 1 with a blue Kessil lamp under an N2 atmosphere at 23 °C produced a color change from dark red to dark brown over the course of minutes. The EPR spectrum of the solution following 10 minutes of irradiation exhibited an isotropic signal with giso = 2.034, identical to the spectrum observed for authentic 3 (Scheme 4b). This observation demonstrates that visible photonic energy induces dissociation of the dimer of 1 to two monomers of 3 by cleavage of one C–C bond and two Ru–N bonds. Continued blue light irradiation of the benzene solution for 3 hours and analysis by 1H NMR spectroscopy revealed formation of 2 along with a new, diamagnetic compound identified as the piano-stool ruthenium complex arising from double hydrogen atom abstractions including the methyl backbone of PmIm (4) similar to a previously reported rhodium example.10 Interestingly, an in situ generated 1:1 mixture of 2 and 4 slowly regenerated 1 under dark, thermal conditions at 23 °C (Scheme 4a). Based on these observations, photoactivation of 1 generated 2 and 4 in an endergonic process that are derived from 3. The reverse reaction occurred under thermal conditions and generated 1, demonstrating a kinetically accessible pathway for C–C bond formation between the two supporting ligands. Although the reversible ligand coupling of the redox-active ligand by stoichiometric chemical oxidants and reductants has previously been reported,52,53 observation of photoswitchable, reversible C–C bond cleavage is unprecedented and highlights the unique properties of the redox-active PmIm ligand.

Scheme 4. (a) Reversible C–C bond cleavage in piano-stool ruthenium complexes. (b) X-band EPR spectrum of the reaction mixture from 1 under photoirradiation for 10 min at 23 °C in benzene.

An independent synthesis of 4 was accomplished by irradiation of a benzene solution of 1 with a blue Kessil lamp in the presence of TEMPO for 18 hours and the desired product was isolated in 51% yield (Scheme 5a). The solid-state structure of 4 was determined by X-ray diffraction and unlike the related rhodium complex that dimerized following H-atom abstraction from the imine methyl group,24 no dimerization was observed (Scheme 5b). Two hydrogen atoms of the methylene (C20–C21 1.348(2) Å) in the backbone were located in the difference map. The Ru–N bonds in 4 (N1–Ru1 2.002(1) Å and N2–Ru1 2.098(1) Å) are significantly shorter than those in 1 (N1–Ru1 2.149(2) Å and N2–Ru1 2.1474(18) Å) as well as a larger bond angle of N1–Ru1–N2 (77.77(4) °) of 4 compared to that of 1 (75.94(8) °). These metrics indicate strong coordination of th PmIm ligand in 4 likely due to its higher covalency as the L,Xtype chelate. Scheme 5. Exploration of Catalytic Element-Hydrogen Bond Formation by Hydrogen Atom Transfer. To explore the utility of 2 in catalytic hydrogen atom transfer chemistry, formation of element-hydrogen bonds using H2 as the terminal reductant was pursued. Inspired by regeneration of 2 from 3 by addition of H2 as the hydrogen atom source, catalytic hydrogenation of TEMPO using 2 as the catalyst was investigated (Scheme 6). When 10 mol% 2 was used as a catalyst under 4 atm H2, TEMPO–H was obtained in 86% yield as judged by NMR spectroscopy after 48 h at 23 °C (Scheme 6).

Scheme 6. Catalytic hydrogenation of TEMPO using 2 as the catalyst.

Encouraged by the successful catalytic hydrogenation of TEMPO by 2, a more challenging substrate was targeted. N–H bond formation was of interest due to the relevance in synthetic cycles for the synthesis of ammonia from its elements.8-11,54-56 Azobenzene has been used as a representative substrate to evaluate stoichiometric HAT reactivity of metal hydrides57,58 but catalytic examples using H2 as the terminal reductant have not been demonstrated. DFT calculations established a low first N–H BDFE of 48.0 kcal/mol with a higher second N–H BDFE of 61.4 kcal/mol in acetonitrile en route to 1,2- diphenylhydrazine formation (Scheme 7a). Peters and coworkers recently reported that [(η5-C5Me5)Fe(dppe)H] (dppe = 1,2-bis(diphenylphosphino)ethane) has an Fe–H BDFE of 56 kcal/mol and was unreactive for the reduction of azobenzene. Carbonylation of this compound generated [(η4-C5Me5H)Fe(dppe)(CO)] which was competent for stoichiometric hydrogen atom transfer to form azobenzene. This chemistry is promoted by the low C–H BDFEs of 25-29 kcal/mol, but regeneration by addition of H2 was not reported.57

Because 2 has a relatively weak Ru–H bond of 47.9 kcal/mol and is competent for the activation of dihydrogen, the catalytic reduction of azobenzene using H2 as the terminal reductant seemed plausible. Addition of two equivalents of 2 to a benzene solution of azobenzene generated 78% of diphenylhydrazine and 11% of aniline after 18 hours at 23 °C. In addition, 1 was observed in 65% conversion by 1H NMR spectroscopy (Scheme 7b). Using the same conditions used in the catalytic hydrogenation of TEMPO, azobenzene underwent to hydrogenation to diphenylhydrazine in 61% yield along with 11% of aniline under 4 atm H2 at 23 °C (Scheme 7c). The conditions are milder than those reported previously where well-defined metal complexes promote the catalytic hydrogenation of azobenzene to aniline as the major product owing to the high temperatures and H2 pressures required for activity.59-61 These results demonstrate that 2 is catalytically competent for selective reduction of unsaturated bonds by HAT in cases where more traditional catalytic hydrogenation catalysts are unsuccesful.62,63 Scheme 7. (a) DFT-calculated N–H BDFEs relevant to the formation of 1,2-diphenylhydrazine from hydrogenation of azobenzene. (b) Stochiometric HAT to reduce azobenzene to diphenylhydrazine using two equivalents of 2. (c) Selective hydrogenation of azobenzene to diphenylhydrazine using 2 as the catalyst.

Two additional substrates, acridine and [(tBumPNP)Co(NMes)] (tBumPNP = modified PNP pincer ligand) were evaluated for catalytic N–H bond formation (Scheme 8). Although catalytic hydrogenation of these substrates have been previously investigated with [(η5-C5Me5)Ir(N,C)H]  compounds as bifunctional photocatalysts, thermal reactions in the absence of light did not produce turnover due to high Ir–H BDFEs (60 kcal/mol) that are insufficient to form the N–H BDFEs of these substrates (44.0 and 41.3 kcal/mol in toluene, respectively).13 Using 10 mol% of 2 as the pre-catalyst, hydrogenation of acridine at 60 °C generated the acridine dimer and dihydroacridine as the products in 46% isolated yield and 38% NMR yield, respectively, while the reaction at room temperature  produced only 42% conversion for 48 h (Scheme 8a). Formation of the acridine dimer is consistent with generation of the acridinyl radical, supporting HAT reactivity. Control experiments demonstrate that the metal-nitrogen bond is unreactive toward H2 in the absence of a metal co-catalyst with competing insertion into the metal-phosphorous bond as reported previously.64 This result demonstrates that 2 forms N–H bonds as low as 40 kcal/mol, values inaccessible by the previous [(η5- C5Me5)M(N,C)H] catalysts that are enabled by the low Ru–H BDFE arising from the redox-active PmIm ligand.

CONCLUSION A ruthenium monohydride complex bearing a redox-active pyrimidine-imine chelate has been synthesized. Owing to its relatively low bond dissociation free energy, catalytic reduction of various nitrogen-containing molecules using H2 as the stoichiometric hydrogen atom source under mild reaction conditions was achieved. The ruthenium monohydride was obtained from an isolated diruthenium compound bridged by a C–C bond from the redox-active PmIm chelate. The ruthenium hydride was accessed both thermally and photochemically involving the formation of the mononuclear 17-electron species. Overall, these findings demonstrate a new catalyst design principle for the synthesis of metal hydride catalysts with improved thermal and photochemical stability that serve the dual purpose of H2 activation and subsequent hydrogen atom transfer for the formation of weak chemical bonds.
